I am an old man who has farmed these alkaline alluvial soils of Quzhou for more than fifty years. I finished high school, which was rare for a village boy in my time, so I have always paid close attention to the county agricultural extension bulletins and tried to farm with my head as well as my hands. My family has six mu of good flat land in the North China Plain, and at seventy-two I still make the decisions, though my sons help me hire the machinery services.

It is the middle of April. My winter wheat went into the ground last October, and right now it is in the jointing stage. I will not change crops mid-stream; the wheat stays. I will irrigate it once more at heading and again at grain filling if the weather stays dry, and I will spray a fungicide and one more herbicide before harvest in early June. After the wheat comes off, I will immediately plant summer maize using no-tillage direct seeding. That is the standard double-cropping system here, and it is the only way to get two crops a year on this land. I use an improved wheat variety—Liangxing or Shimai type—because they yield reliably and resist lodging, and I always buy hybrid maize seed such as Nongda 372 or Denghai 605; the hybrid vigor is worth the price. For fertilizer, I apply compound fertilizer as a base and top-dress with urea. I keep my nitrogen a bit lower than some of my neighbors because I know too much N makes the wheat lodge and wastes money, but I maintain enough phosphorus and potassium to keep the soil fertile. I also return all the straw to the field to keep the organic matter up.
